events.title: Germ Theory of Fermentation Established
events.blurb: A French chemist demonstrated through carefully controlled experiments that fermentation and putrefaction were caused by specific living microorganisms rather than by spontaneous chemical processes, and that sterilising a broth and sealing it from the air could prevent spoilage indefinitely. The experiments demolished the theory of spontaneous generation and formed the empirical backbone of germ theory.
events.revealBlurb: 1859–1861 — Louis Pasteur's famous swan-neck flask experiments showed that sterilized broth stayed clear indefinitely until the curved neck was broken, letting airborne microbes in. He reportedly presented one surviving flask to the Academy in 1878 saying it had shown no signs of life in fifteen years. Some of those original flasks are still intact at the Pasteur Institute.

events.title: X-Rays Discovered
events.blurb: While experimenting with cathode ray tubes in a darkened laboratory, a German physicist noticed that a fluorescent screen across the room glowed even though it was shielded from the tube's visible light. The mysterious new rays penetrated cardboard, wood, and flesh, but were blocked by dense metal. Within weeks he had produced the first medical radiograph, showing the bones of his wife's hand.
events.revealBlurb: November 8, 1895 — Wilhelm Röntgen kept the discovery secret for seven weeks, repeating every experiment before telling anyone. He named the rays "X" because he didn't know what they were. He won the very first Nobel Prize in Physics in 1901 and donated the prize money to his university.

events.title: Special Relativity Paper Published
events.blurb: A 30-page paper demolished the concept of absolute time, arguing that the speed of light is the same for all observers regardless of their motion, and that simultaneity, length, and mass all depend on relative velocity. The paper contained no citations, because its author — a patent clerk working in his spare time — had arrived at the theory by pure thought experiment.
events.revealBlurb: September 26, 1905 — one of four papers the same author submitted to Annalen der Physik that year, including one on Brownian motion and one that would later win the Nobel Prize for the photoelectric effect. The mass-energy equivalence paper (E=mc²) followed two months later.

events.title: General Relativity Confirmed by Eclipse
events.blurb: Two British expeditions sent to observe a total solar eclipse measured the positions of stars near the Sun's edge and found their apparent positions had shifted by an amount predicted by a new theory of gravitation — confirming that massive objects warp the fabric of space itself. The results overturned the classical picture of gravity as a force acting at a distance and made the paper's author internationally famous overnight.
events.revealBlurb: November 6, 1919 — Arthur Eddington announced the results to a packed joint meeting of the Royal Society and Royal Astronomical Society in London. The Times headline read "Revolution in Science." Some later scholars questioned the data quality, but multiple subsequent eclipses fully confirmed the result.

events.title: Endosymbiotic Theory Published
events.blurb: A paper proposed that the energy-producing mitochondria and photosynthetic chloroplasts inside complex cells were originally free-living bacteria that had been engulfed by a host cell and retained over billions of years — a radical claim that the cell's most vital structures were once independent organisms. The paper had been rejected by approximately fifteen journals before finding a publisher.
events.revealBlurb: June 1967 — Lynn Margulis submitted the paper under her married surname Sagan; it became one of biology's most-cited papers after decades of derision. Her critics called it "too fantastic." When the hypothesis was tested by comparing DNA in mitochondria to bacterial DNA in the 1980s, it matched almost exactly.

events.title: First Animal in Earth Orbit
events.blurb: A stray mixed-breed dog named Laika became the first living creature to orbit Earth when the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 2, a 508 kg spacecraft with no reentry capability. Laika survived liftoff and initial orbit but died from overheating within five to seven hours when a thermal regulation system failed — a fact withheld from the public for decades.
events.revealBlurb: November 3, 1957 — Sputnik 2. The Soviets announced Laika died painlessly after several days; the truth wasn't confirmed until 2002. The spacecraft had been built in under four weeks on Khrushchev's orders to celebrate the 40th anniversary of the October Revolution. Laika has since been honored with a monument in Moscow and a postage stamp in more than 70 countries.

events.title: First Mars Close-Up Flyby
events.blurb: Mariner 4 flew within 9,846 km of Mars and transmitted 21 photographs covering about 1% of the planet's surface — the first close-range images of another planet. The images revealed a cratered, Moon-like landscape and showed Mars had a much thinner atmosphere than expected, with a surface pressure of roughly 4–7 millibars, dashing hopes of a habitable world.
events.revealBlurb: July 14, 1965 — Mariner 4. The images took four days to receive and were so eagerly anticipated that JPL technicians printed the first strips of data by hand onto paper using artist's pastels, coloring by number before the computer could process the file. The result was a blurry colored rectangle they pinned to a bulletin board.

events.title: ISS First Crewed Occupation
events.blurb: A three-person crew docked a Soyuz capsule to the International Space Station's Zvezda module at 09:21 UTC, beginning a continuous human presence in low Earth orbit that has not been interrupted since. The station at that point consisted of three connected modules spanning roughly 27 meters, a fraction of its eventual 109-meter length.
events.revealBlurb: November 2, 2000 — Expedition 1. Commander Bill Shepherd radioed NASA to request the station's call sign be changed from "Alpha" to "International Space Station" — a small act of diplomacy that stuck. The crew of two Russians and one American had access to less than 425 cubic meters of living space, about the volume of a large school bus.

events.title: Mir Space Station Deorbit
events.blurb: Russia deliberately deorbited the Mir space station after 15 years of continuous operation, using three burns from a docked Progress cargo spacecraft to lower its orbit until it reentered the atmosphere over the South Pacific. Most of the station burned up during reentry, but approximately 1,500 kg of debris survived and splashed into the ocean between Australia and Chile.
events.revealBlurb: March 23, 2001 — Mir deorbit. Mir had been in orbit so long that cosmonauts reported the walls were alive with mold. A Russian company sold pay-per-view rights to watch the reentry from a chartered aircraft. Japan offered to purchase and keep the station operational; the deal fell through over cost. It had been visited by 104 cosmonauts and astronauts from 12 nations.

events.title: First Orbital Rocket Booster Landing
events.blurb: A SpaceX Falcon 9 first stage returned from an orbital-class mission and landed upright at Landing Zone 1 in Cape Canaveral, completing the first successful recovery of an orbital-class rocket booster under propulsive control. The same vehicle had delivered 11 commercial satellites to orbit minutes earlier and touched down within about 10 meters of the target pad.
events.revealBlurb: December 21, 2015 — OG-2 Mission 2. SpaceX had attempted and failed four previous booster landings on a drone ship at sea. The Falcon's legs deployed at 180 m altitude. Elon Musk posted one word after confirmation: "Welcome back, baby." The reused booster concept cut launch costs by roughly 30%.

events.title: Hippocratic Oath Composed
events.blurb: Greek medical writers associated with a physician teaching on an Aegean island composed a short ethical oath addressed to Apollo and Asclepius, binding physicians to care for their patients, respect their teachers, preserve patient confidences, and do no harm. The document is arguably the oldest surviving code of professional ethics. Modern versions, substantially modified, are still sworn by many medical-school graduates.
events.revealBlurb: c. 400 BCE — attributed to Hippocrates of Kos, though probably composed by his students or school. The modern "first, do no harm" is actually not in the original Greek text; it appears later in Hippocrates' Epidemics. The oath still shows up at white-coat ceremonies.

events.title: Nightingale at Scutari
events.blurb: A 34-year-old British nurse arrived with 38 volunteer nurses at a filthy military hospital in a former Turkish barracks outside a Bosphorus capital, where British wounded from a Crimean war were dying of typhus, cholera, and dysentery at far higher rates than from combat wounds. Her reforms — sanitation, proper food, hand-washing, laundry — cut the death rate from 42 percent to 2 percent in six months. Her subsequent statistical advocacy reshaped nursing as a profession.
events.revealBlurb: November 4, 1854 — Florence Nightingale at Scutari (now Üsküdar, Istanbul). Her nighttime rounds with an oil lamp produced the "Lady with the Lamp" sobriquet. She returned to London with chronic brucellosis, spent most of the rest of her life bedridden, and still wrote 200 books and reports. She lived to 90.

events.title: Röntgen Discovers X-Rays
events.blurb: A 50-year-old German physicist, working with a cathode-ray tube covered in black cardboard, noticed that a paper screen coated in barium platinocyanide glowed even when placed some distance away. He realized the tube was emitting an invisible, unknown type of radiation. Further experiments showed the rays penetrated paper, wood, aluminum, and even human flesh — but not bone. He published an image of his wife's hand, showing her skeleton and wedding ring.
events.revealBlurb: November 8, 1895 — Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen at the University of Würzburg. He called the phenomenon "X" rays because he didn't know what they were. He won the first Nobel Prize in Physics in 1901. The image of his wife's hand, published in early 1896, is arguably the first diagnostic X-ray.

events.title: Aspirin Marketed
events.blurb: A German pharmaceutical and dye company began commercial sales of acetylsalicylic acid tablets under a trade name they had registered, marketed initially as an analgesic and anti-inflammatory. The active compound had been synthesized decades earlier, but this company had developed a stable, pure form suitable for mass production. The drug became one of the best-selling over-the-counter medications in history; low-dose versions are now used preventively against cardiovascular disease.
events.revealBlurb: March 6, 1899 — Bayer AG. Chief chemist Felix Hoffmann is traditionally credited; some historians credit Arthur Eichengrün, a Jewish colleague whose role was erased under Nazi-era Bayer PR. The drug's trade name came from a combination of "acetyl" and Spiraea, a plant source of salicylic acid.

events.title: Fleming Discovers Penicillin
events.blurb: A 47-year-old Scottish bacteriologist returning from a summer holiday to his London laboratory noticed that one of the staphylococcus-culture plates he had left stacked on his bench had been contaminated by a mold, and that a clear zone of inhibition around the mold showed the bacteria had died there. He identified the mold genus, isolated an anti-bacterial substance it produced, and published his findings — which were largely ignored for over a decade.
events.revealBlurb: September 28, 1928 — Alexander Fleming at St Mary's Hospital, London. Howard Florey and Ernst Chain at Oxford successfully purified penicillin in 1941, making it a usable drug. They shared the 1945 Nobel with Fleming. The drug's mass production during WWII saved hundreds of thousands of Allied soldiers' lives.

events.title: Lascaux Cave Paintings
events.blurb: In a limestone complex in southwestern France, Paleolithic artists over multiple generations painted some 6,000 bulls, deer, horses, and abstract signs along narrow corridors and a soaring "Hall of the Bulls" as large as a Romanesque nave. The largest painted bull is over five metres long. The cave was rediscovered in 1940 by four teenagers and their dog investigating a tree that had been uprooted by a storm.
events.revealBlurb: c. 17,000 BCE — Montignac, Dordogne. The original cave was closed to visitors in 1963 when tourist breath and carbon dioxide began damaging the pigments. Lascaux II, III, and IV — increasingly faithful replicas — have been opened to the public.

events.title: Tutankhamun Death Mask Created
events.blurb: Egyptian craftsmen fashioned a 10.2-kilogram gold funerary mask inlaid with lapis lazuli, carnelian, obsidian, and coloured glass to cover the mummy of a teenage pharaoh who had died at 18. The mask was sealed in a tomb packed with over 5,000 objects. The boy-king had been a minor figure; the tomb escaped the looting that emptied nearly every other Egyptian royal burial. It was untouched for 3,245 years.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1323 BCE — Tutankhamun died. Howard Carter's team uncovered the tomb on November 4, 1922. The mask now spends most of its time in a Cairo museum case and has been on world tours twice. The beard fell off during cleaning in 2014 and was hastily reattached with epoxy.

events.title: Vermeer's Girl with a Pearl Earring
events.blurb: A Dutch painter in his early thirties completed an intimate oil study on canvas of a young woman turning toward the viewer, her head covered in a blue and yellow turban, a single teardrop-shaped pearl catching the light at her ear. It was not a commissioned portrait but a "tronie" — a character study. The artist made only about 35 paintings in his career; this one was rediscovered in 1881 at auction for two guilders.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1665 — Johannes Vermeer. Now in the Mauritshuis in The Hague. The "pearl" may actually be tin or glass — no pearl of that size is plausible. Tracy Chevalier's 1999 novel and the 2003 film made it a pop-culture icon.

events.title: Hokusai's Great Wave
events.blurb: A 70-year-old Japanese printmaker produced the first of thirty-six woodblock prints depicting views of a sacred mountain, all showing it from different perspectives and in different weather. The first print, which viewers sometimes mistook for the title piece, showed an enormous wave curling in threatening foam over three small fishing boats, with the mountain a distant cone between its spray. The distinctive blue pigment, Prussian blue, was a recent European import.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1831 — Katsushika Hokusai. The print is one of the most widely reproduced images in the world; thousands of impressions survive. Hokusai called himself "the old man mad about drawing" and claimed he would become a true artist only at 110.

events.title: Mona Lisa Stolen
events.blurb: An Italian handyman who had worked at a Paris museum hid overnight in a storage closet, walked out the next morning in his worker's smock carrying a 77 by 53 cm wooden panel under his arm, and disappeared for two years and four months. The panel was a portrait by Leonardo da Vinci of a Florentine merchant's wife. The theft made worldwide news; Picasso and the poet Apollinaire were briefly questioned as suspects. The picture had been little known until this moment.
events.revealBlurb: August 21, 1911 — Vincenzo Peruggia. He was caught in Florence 28 months later trying to sell it to the Uffizi. He served seven months in Italian prison and was celebrated as a patriot by many Italians. The theft made the Mona Lisa internationally famous.

events.title: Quit India Movement
events.blurb: After the failure of a British mission that offered only a vague promise of post-war dominion status, the Congress party launched a mass movement demanding immediate British withdrawal. The entire leadership was arrested at dawn the following day. The movement went underground and continued for years — sabotage, strikes, alternative governments in remote districts. It was violently suppressed, but British rule was visibly over as a legitimate proposition.
events.revealBlurb: August 8, 1942 — Gandhi's "Do or Die" speech at the Bombay Congress session. Churchill imprisoned 100,000 activists and held the line; by VJ Day in 1945, however, Britain was bankrupt and the political capital to hold India was gone.

events.title: Gandhi Assassinated
events.blurb: A 78-year-old man, walking slowly across a Delhi lawn supported by two of his grandnieces, was shot three times in the chest at point-blank range by a Hindu nationalist who blamed him for indulging Muslims and accepting partition. He fell murmuring the name of a god. He had survived five previous attempts on his life.
events.revealBlurb: January 30, 1948 — the assassin was Nathuram Godse, a former editor of a Hindu nationalist newspaper. He was convicted and executed. Gandhi had warned his secretary that morning that his life's work would not be judged "until after I am dead and gone."

events.title: Emergency Declared
events.blurb: Two weeks after a court had found her guilty of electoral malpractice and barred her from office, a prime minister persuaded the president to declare a state of emergency under the constitution. Opposition leaders were arrested in the night, press censorship imposed, civil liberties suspended, and constitutional amendments rushed through a pliant parliament. The suspension of democracy lasted 21 months and is the darkest interval in the republic's history.
events.revealBlurb: June 25, 1975 — Indira Gandhi. The Emergency was defended in the name of stability; mass sterilizations, slum clearances, and the personality cult of her son Sanjay made it notorious. Ended March 21, 1977.

events.title: Indira Gandhi Assassinated
events.blurb: The prime minister, walking from her bungalow to a garden office for a scheduled interview with a British filmmaker, was shot 31 times at close range by two of her own Sikh bodyguards. She was rushed to a nearby hospital and died during surgery. Four days of anti-Sikh riots followed in the capital, organized partly by politicians of her own party, killing at least 3,000 people. Her son Rajiv was sworn in as prime minister the same evening.
events.revealBlurb: October 31, 1984 — Satwant Singh and Beant Singh, bodyguards who had both been retained despite security concerns after Blue Star. The Justice Nanavati Commission documented the organized nature of the subsequent riots; convictions have come only in the last few years.

events.title: Demonetisation
events.blurb: In a surprise eight-o'clock television address, the prime minister announced that the two largest-denomination banknotes in circulation — 86 percent of all currency by value — would cease to be legal tender at midnight. The stated targets were counterfeit money, black money, and terrorism financing. Long queues formed outside banks for weeks; small businesses and day-labourers, most paid in cash, were disproportionately hit. Subsequent data showed most demonetised cash returned to the banking system.
events.revealBlurb: November 8, 2016 — Narendra Modi. By the Reserve Bank's own accounting, 99.3 percent of the old notes were eventually exchanged. Counterfeit detection was negligible. The policy's effect on corruption is still debated; its effect on GDP was negative.

events.title: Bach Dedicates Brandenburg Concertos
events.blurb: A 36-year-old German court composer, looking for a new job, sent a margrave a set of six concerto grossi he had been accumulating over several years. The dedication was effusive; he apologized for the "vast distance between his person and the margrave." The margrave never acknowledged the gift, let alone hired him, and probably never had them performed. The manuscripts sat in a Prussian archive for 128 years before rediscovery.
events.revealBlurb: March 24, 1721 — Johann Sebastian Bach, addressing Christian Ludwig of Brandenburg. The scores were narrowly rescued from Allied bombing in 1945. The music now exists thanks to a librarian who grabbed them as he fled Leipzig for the Harz mountains.

events.title: Louis Armstrong's Hot Fives
events.blurb: A 24-year-old cornetist who had grown up in the poorest section of New Orleans walked into a Chicago studio for the first session with a small band of his own. Over the next three years, the "Hot Five" and "Hot Seven" sessions would reshape popular music. His vocal improvisation on "Heebie Jeebies" — a chorus of nonsense syllables when he claimed to drop his lyric sheet — launched scat singing. His trumpet solos made the individual improvisation the heart of jazz.
events.revealBlurb: November 12, 1925 — Louis Armstrong at OKeh Records, Chicago. The "Heebie Jeebies" vocal made him a national figure. He would become the first African-American to host a nationally sponsored radio show.

events.title: Beatles' Final Public Performance
events.blurb: A four-piece rock band performed without announcement on the roof of their recording company's London headquarters for 42 minutes in near-freezing winter temperatures, drawing a crowd of hundreds in the street below before police ended the show citing noise complaints. The impromptu rooftop set was their last performance together in front of a live audience.

events.title: Led Zeppelin IV Released
events.blurb: A British rock band released their fourth album with no title, no text, and no band name anywhere on the cover — just a painting of an old man with a bundle of firewood on his back. The album contained eight tracks, including an eight-minute multi-part track that would become the most-played song on American FM radio for a decade. Critics were lukewarm; listeners bought 37 million copies.
events.revealBlurb: November 8, 1971 — Led Zeppelin IV, featuring "Stairway to Heaven." The band was so angered by critical reception of the previous album that they refused to identify themselves on this one. The old man on the cover was a real picture bought from an antique shop in Reading.

events.title: Paul Simon's Graceland Released
events.blurb: A 44-year-old American songwriter released an album recorded largely in Johannesburg studios with South African musicians, fusing American folk and pop with mbaqanga, isicathamiya, and zydeco. The album was controversial: the United Nations had called for a cultural boycott of the apartheid regime, and many considered the recording sessions a violation. The finished record was nonetheless a critical and commercial phenomenon and was credited with exposing mass audiences to South African musical traditions.
events.revealBlurb: August 25, 1986 — Paul Simon. Collaborators included Ladysmith Black Mambazo, Ray Phiri, and the Boyoyo Boys. Simon was blacklisted by the UN but sang in Zimbabwe and Zambia; Nelson Mandela later thanked him for the cultural bridge.

events.title: Susan B. Anthony Votes
events.blurb: A 52-year-old suffragist and 14 other women presented themselves at a polling place in their upstate New York city and demanded to register to vote, citing the language of the recently ratified 14th Amendment. Three inspectors, after consulting the U.S. constitution, let them register. On election day four days later she voted; she was arrested two weeks after that. Her trial, the following year, denied her the right to testify in her own defense.
events.revealBlurb: November 5, 1872 — Rochester, NY. Judge Ward Hunt fined her $100; she refused ever to pay. The U.S. has since put her face on a coin that was widely disliked and quickly withdrawn (the 1979 dollar).

events.title: Marie Curie Wins Nobel Prize
events.blurb: A 36-year-old Polish-born physicist working in a converted shed in a French capital became the first woman to win the world's most prestigious scientific prize, sharing a physics award with her husband and a French colleague for their research into radioactivity. She would win it a second time, alone, in chemistry eight years later. Her notebooks are still radioactive, stored in lead-lined boxes and read only in protective clothing.
events.revealBlurb: December 10, 1903 — shared with Pierre Curie and Henri Becquerel. She later became the first person, of any gender, to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences. Her daughter Irène won a Nobel in chemistry too.

events.title: Jeannette Rankin Elected to Congress
events.blurb: A 36-year-old social worker and suffrage organizer from a western U.S. state was elected to the U.S. House of Representatives, becoming the first woman to hold federal office in the country. She took office four years before women nationally could vote. She would vote against entering both world wars — the only member of Congress to do so twice.
events.revealBlurb: November 7, 1916 — Montana had given women the state vote in 1914. Rankin's 1941 "no" vote on the declaration of war against Japan made her a pariah; she had to be escorted to her office by the Capitol police. "As a woman I can't go to war," she said, "and I refuse to send anyone else."

events.title: FDA Approves the Pill
events.blurb: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved a daily oral contraceptive pill combining synthetic estrogen and progestin for sale as a birth-control product, two years after approving the same drug for menstrual disorders. Over two million American women were taking it within three years. It was the first drug ever developed for use by healthy people rather than sick ones, and it reshaped women's labour-force participation for the next half-century.
events.revealBlurb: May 9, 1960 — Enovid, made by G.D. Searle. The research had been funded privately by heiress Katharine McCormick because federal funding was politically impossible. Single women could be denied prescriptions until a 1972 Supreme Court ruling.

events.title: Margaret Thatcher Becomes PM
events.blurb: The leader of the British Conservative Party, a grocer's daughter who had studied chemistry at Oxford and later trained as a barrister, was invited by the monarch to form a government after her party won a sweeping parliamentary majority. She became the United Kingdom's first woman prime minister and would hold the office for 11 years — the longest continuous premiership of the 20th century.
events.revealBlurb: May 4, 1979 — she took office quoting St. Francis of Assisi on the doorstep: "Where there is discord, may we bring harmony." The next decade would be anything but that. She was forced to resign by her own cabinet in November 1990.

events.title: Columbus Reaches the Americas
events.blurb: A Genoese navigator captaining three small Spanish ships, after 33 days of open-Atlantic sailing from the Canary Islands with an increasingly mutinous crew, sighted land just after 2 AM — a low-lying island he promptly named after a Christian saviour. He was convinced, and would die still convinced, that he had reached the outer islands of Asia. The four voyages he made over the next twelve years reshaped two continents.
events.revealBlurb: October 12, 1492 — Christopher Columbus made landfall on Guanahani in the Bahamas. The lookout who first sighted land, Rodrigo de Triana, did not receive the promised reward — Columbus claimed he had seen a light the previous evening. The contact collapsed Indigenous populations via epidemic disease within decades.

events.title: Cortés Reaches Tenochtitlán
events.blurb: A 34-year-old Spanish conquistador, in defiance of orders from the governor of Cuba who had tried to recall him, entered the causeway-linked lakeside capital of the Aztec Triple Alliance — a city of perhaps 200,000 people, one of the largest in the world, built on an island in a high-altitude lake. The Aztec emperor met him with courtesy, gifts, and quiet suspicion. Within two years the emperor would be dead and the city in ruins.
events.revealBlurb: November 8, 1519 — Hernán Cortés meets Moctezuma II in Tenochtitlán (modern Mexico City). The Spanish force was about 500 strong, augmented by thousands of Tlaxcalan allies who hated the Aztecs. Cortés had burned his own ships on the coast to prevent desertion.

events.title: Spanish Armada Defeated
events.blurb: A Spanish naval force of 130 ships and 26,000 men, intended to escort a Flemish invasion army across the Channel to England, was met by a faster, more maneuverable English fleet off the Flanders coast. An English fireship attack scattered the Spanish anchorage overnight; the following day's running battle crippled the armada. Storms in the North Sea and along the Irish coast destroyed the rest on the long retreat home. Barely half returned to Spain.
events.revealBlurb: July 29 to August 8, 1588 — Battle of Gravelines decided it. English commanders: Lord Howard of Effingham, Sir Francis Drake. Roughly 35 Spanish ships reached home; most of the rest were wrecked on the Irish coast, whose people dealt harshly with survivors.

events.title: Shakespeare's First Folio
events.blurb: Seven years after the Stratford-born playwright's death, two of his fellow actors compiled and published a folio edition of 36 of his plays — 18 of which had never been printed before. Without the volume, half the plays, including Macbeth, Julius Caesar, and The Tempest, would have been lost. 750 copies were printed; 235 are known to survive today, fetching tens of millions at auction.
events.revealBlurb: November 8, 1623 — compiled by John Heminges and Henry Condell. It was sold for £1 — roughly £200 today. A recently discovered copy was unmasked at a Scottish library in 2016. The folio standardized the canonical text of most of the plays.

events.title: Peace of Westphalia
events.blurb: Two treaties negotiated simultaneously at two Westphalian cities ended the Thirty Years War in Germany and the Eighty Years War between Spain and the Dutch Republic. 235 delegations from across Europe had been meeting for four years. The settlement recognized the sovereign equality of European states, gave rulers the right to determine the religion of their own territories, and acknowledged Dutch and Swiss independence. Historians often date the modern state system from here.
events.revealBlurb: October 24, 1648 — treaties signed at Münster and Osnabrück. The war had killed an estimated eight million people, roughly 20 percent of the German population. The phrase "Westphalian sovereignty" still refers to the principle of non-intervention in internal affairs of other states.

events.title: Truman Doctrine
events.blurb: Addressing a joint session of Congress, a U.S. president requested $400 million in aid for Greece and Turkey and announced a sweeping new foreign policy: the United States would support "free peoples" resisting armed minorities or outside pressures. The speech committed America to global containment of communism.
events.revealBlurb: March 12, 1947 — Harry Truman needed just 18 minutes. Behind the rhetoric: Britain, bankrupted by war, had quietly told Washington it could no longer prop up the Greek government. America stepped into the imperial vacuum.

events.title: First Soviet Atomic Bomb Test
events.blurb: Four years after U.S. weapons ended the Pacific war, Soviet scientists detonated their own plutonium implosion device at a test range in the Kazakh steppe. Western intelligence had predicted the breakthrough was at least five years away. The explosion ended the American nuclear monopoly and opened the arms race.
events.revealBlurb: August 29, 1949 — codename RDS-1, nicknamed "First Lightning." The design was largely cribbed from the U.S. Fat Man bomb via spy networks inside the Manhattan Project. Klaus Fuchs had handed over detailed blueprints.

events.title: Gorbachev Becomes Soviet Leader
events.blurb: After three elderly Soviet leaders died in rapid succession, a 54-year-old party functionary with a law degree and a distinctive birthmark on his forehead was elected General Secretary. Within months he was speaking publicly about "glasnost" (openness) and "perestroika" (restructuring). His colleagues had picked him hoping for energetic continuity. They got revolution.
events.revealBlurb: March 11, 1985 — Mikhail Gorbachev, the youngest Politburo member. Foreign Minister Andrei Gromyko, who nominated him, said: "Comrades, this man has a nice smile, but he has iron teeth." Gorbachev won the Nobel Peace Prize five years later.

events.title: Berlin Wall Falls
events.blurb: An East German government spokesman announced at a press conference that citizens could cross the border immediately, triggering jubilant crowds who arrived at checkpoints and began dismantling the 155-kilometre concrete barrier with hammers and their bare hands. More than two million East Germans crossed into West Berlin during the following weekend alone.

events.title: Fall of the Berlin Wall
events.blurb: An East German spokesman, reading hastily from a note and misunderstanding its contents, announced at a televised press conference that new travel rules would take effect "immediately." Within hours, tens of thousands of jubilant East Berliners massed at the crossings. Confused border guards, receiving no clear orders, simply let them through. People scrambled onto the concrete barrier with hammers.
events.revealBlurb: November 9, 1989 — the spokesman was Günter Schabowski, who had skimmed the briefing note just before the press conference. Asked when the rules took effect, he shrugged: "As far as I know — immediately." The wall, built in a single night 28 years earlier, came down in a single night too.

events.title: UNIVAC Predicts Election
events.blurb: A televised presidential election broadcast featured, as a novelty, a commercial digital computer that had been sold to the Census Bureau six months earlier. Fed early returns by its operators, the machine predicted an Eisenhower landslide hours before conventional forecasters were willing to call the race. CBS' broadcasters initially didn't trust it and understated its projection on-air. The machine was right.
events.revealBlurb: November 4, 1952 — UNIVAC I, on CBS. The machine predicted 438 electoral votes for Eisenhower; the actual result was 442. After the election, CBS' on-air introducer Charles Collingwood admitted they had held back UNIVAC's early call for fear it would look ridiculous.

events.title: Intel 4004 Microprocessor Released
events.blurb: Intel released a 4-bit central processing unit containing 2,300 transistors on a silicon chip the size of a fingernail, capable of 60,000 operations per second. Originally designed for a Japanese calculator company, it became the world's first commercially available microprocessor — the prototype for every CPU that followed.

events.title: Apple Computer Founded
events.blurb: Two 20-something Californians, a college dropout and a self-taught engineer, formed a partnership to sell a printed-circuit-board computer design the engineer had developed and the dropout had realized was marketable. A third partner, older and more cautious, asked out within two weeks and sold his share back for $800. The initial product was a hand-built board requiring the buyer to supply their own power supply, keyboard, and case.
events.revealBlurb: April 1, 1976 — Steve Jobs, Steve Wozniak, and Ronald Wayne. Wayne's 10 percent share would today be worth over $300 billion. He has said he doesn't regret selling out; he'd been in a startup before and wanted to avoid another personal-liability exposure.

events.title: Sony Walkman Released
events.blurb: A Japanese electronics company released a portable personal cassette player, weighing 390 grams, with headphones instead of a speaker. It had no record function — unusual for a cassette player — and its CEO personally insisted on this as a way of encouraging private, solitary music consumption. The device created an entirely new product category and pulled portable listening out of the car radio and boombox and into the individual's pocket for the next quarter-century.
events.revealBlurb: July 1, 1979 — Sony TPS-L2. Co-founder Masaru Ibuka had wanted something compact to enjoy opera on long flights. The original name in Japan was "Walkman"; in the US, "Soundabout"; in the UK, "Stowaway." "Walkman" eventually won out globally.

events.title: Google Founded
events.blurb: Two Stanford doctoral students incorporated a search engine company whose name derived from the mathematical term for 10 to the power of 100. Their PageRank algorithm ranked results by treating hyperlinks as votes, producing more relevant results than the keyword-frequency systems that dominated at the time.

events.title: American Idol Premieres
events.blurb: A singing-competition reality show — adapted from a British format — premiered on Fox with a caustic British music executive as its lead judge, flanked by two milder American ones. The first season's audition rounds and final contestant-viewer-vote format drew enormous audiences; its first winner, a 20-year-old Texan waitress, became a genuine pop star. The show's stern British judge became a cultural shorthand for merciless critique.
events.revealBlurb: June 11, 2002 — judges Simon Cowell, Paula Abdul, Randy Jackson. Host Ryan Seacrest. Season 1 winner Kelly Clarkson went on to a successful music and TV career. American Idol ran on Fox until 2016 and was revived on ABC in 2018; Clarkson's "A Moment Like This" is still its most famous product.

events.title: William and Kate Wedding
events.blurb: The 28-year-old second-in-line heir to the British throne married his 29-year-old university sweetheart at Westminster Abbey in London before a congregation of 1,900 and a global TV audience estimated at 2 billion. The bride wore a long-sleeved ivory lace gown; the couple kissed twice on the Buckingham Palace balcony. The marriage, closely followed by the British tabloids for years, has so far produced three children and remained notably less turbulent than the equivalent royal marriage of the generation before.
events.revealBlurb: April 29, 2011 — Prince William and Catherine Middleton. William succeeded his father Charles as Prince of Wales when Charles became king in September 2022. Their three children, in line to the throne: George (2013), Charlotte (2015), Louis (2018).

events.title: Osama bin Laden Killed
events.blurb: A team of US Navy SEALs, helicoptered into the Pakistani city of Abbottabad at night, stormed a walled compound where the founder of al-Qaeda had been hiding for over five years, 1.3 kilometres from Pakistan's premier military academy. He was killed in the raid, along with four others. His body was buried at sea from a US carrier to prevent his grave becoming a pilgrimage site. The president announced the operation in a late-night television address; crowds gathered outside the White House chanting "USA."
events.revealBlurb: May 2, 2011 — Operation Neptune Spear. SEAL Team Six; President Barack Obama. Bin Laden had orchestrated the September 11, 2001 attacks. His death ended a 9-year, 8-month manhunt. The compound was demolished months later by the Pakistani government.

events.title: Kim Kardashian "Breaks the Internet"
events.blurb: A 34-year-old reality TV star and entrepreneur appeared on the cover of a magazine nude, balancing a champagne glass on her bared posterior, with a headline directly daring the internet to be broken by it. The cover image was shared widely enough that the magazine's website crashed for short periods. The photograph — shot by a French photographer who had staged similar images four decades earlier — launched weeks of commentary about sexuality, race, body image, and the limits of viral marketing.
events.revealBlurb: November 11, 2014 — Kim Kardashian on Paper magazine. Photographer Jean-Paul Goude had shot nearly identical images with other models in the 1970s and 80s, drawing accusations that he specifically emphasized and sexualized Black bodies. The cover did, in fact, briefly break the magazine's website.

events.title: Harambe Killed
events.blurb: A 17-year-old western lowland gorilla at the Cincinnati Zoo was shot and killed by zoo staff after a 3-year-old boy climbed through a barrier and fell into the gorilla enclosure. The zoo explained that the gorilla had grabbed the child and dragged him through the water; tranquilizer darts would have taken too long. The killing triggered a wave of online outrage, internet memes, and several years' worth of "RIP Harambe" jokes that became a meta-joke of 2010s internet culture.
events.revealBlurb: May 28, 2016 — Harambe, Cincinnati Zoo. The child recovered fully. The zoo director Thane Maynard defended the decision as the only available option. The Harambe meme's peculiar staying power has been studied as a case of absurdist internet grief; election-poll write-in votes for Harambe persisted for years.

events.title: Great Lisbon Earthquake
events.blurb: On the morning of a major Catholic holy day, a magnitude-9 earthquake struck off the Atlantic coast of a European capital while most residents were at Mass. The quake was followed within 40 minutes by a tsunami that rolled up the Tagus River, and a citywide fire that burned for five days. Roughly 40,000 of the city's 200,000 inhabitants died.
events.revealBlurb: November 1, 1755 — All Saints' Day in Lisbon. Voltaire wrote his anti-optimist poem about it, then Candide. The Portuguese prime minister, the Marquis of Pombal, supposedly asked "What now? We bury the dead and feed the living" and rebuilt the city on a grid.

events.title: Spanish Flu Pandemic Begins
events.blurb: An unusually lethal strain of influenza, carried through military camps and troop ships during the final months of a world war, infected a third of the planet and killed an estimated 50 to 100 million people in three successive waves over two years. Unlike most flus, it disproportionately killed healthy young adults by triggering cytokine storms in robust immune systems.
events.revealBlurb: March 1918 — first identified at a US Army base in Kansas. It was called "Spanish" only because wartime censorship in belligerent countries suppressed coverage; neutral Spain reported it freely, so it seemed to originate there. It had nothing to do with Spain.

events.title: Bhola Cyclone
events.blurb: A tropical cyclone with 185 km/h winds made landfall on the low-lying islands of the Bay of Bengal delta at high tide, driving a 10-metre storm surge over villages built at sea level. At least 300,000 people died, possibly up to 500,000 — the deadliest tropical cyclone in recorded history. The East Pakistan government's slow response fueled the separatist movement that led to war within months.
events.revealBlurb: November 12, 1970 — East Pakistan (now Bangladesh). The relief failure helped trigger the Bangladesh Liberation War the following March. The former Beatle George Harrison organized the Concert for Bangladesh to raise funds.

events.title: Hurricane Katrina
events.blurb: A Category 3 hurricane made landfall on the US Gulf Coast, driving a storm surge that overtopped and breached the levee system protecting a major port city lying largely below sea level. 80 percent of the city flooded; 1,392 people died. The chaotic federal response — images of thousands stranded on a sports stadium roof, bodies floating in water — inflicted lasting damage on the administration in power.
events.revealBlurb: August 29, 2005 — New Orleans, Louisiana. The Superdome housed 30,000 evacuees for five days in deteriorating conditions. The head of FEMA, Michael Brown, had previously run the International Arabian Horse Association; he resigned within two weeks.

events.title: Typhoon Haiyan
events.blurb: One of the strongest tropical cyclones ever recorded at landfall — with sustained winds of 315 km/h — struck the central Philippines, obliterating coastal cities. A 7-metre storm surge drove ships onto city streets; the city of Tacloban lost most of its infrastructure. At least 6,300 people died, and 4 million were displaced.
events.revealBlurb: November 8, 2013 — Leyte province. The Filipino lead negotiator at the UN climate talks that week gave a tearful speech and began a hunger strike until "meaningful progress" was made. His country's delegation wore black.

events.title: Chaucer's Canterbury Tales
events.blurb: An English civil servant in his mid-fifties died leaving unfinished a collection of stories told by pilgrims riding from Southwark to a Kentish cathedral shrine. Written in Middle English rather than French or Latin, the work demonstrated the poetic range of the English vernacular across a social spectrum — knights, millers, cooks, pardoners, the famously bawdy Wife of Bath. Only 24 of a planned 120 tales were ever completed.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1400 — Geoffrey Chaucer. He is often called the father of English literature. Roughly 80 manuscripts survive; the earliest complete ones date from the 1410s. The Wife of Bath's Tale became an early feminist touchstone.

events.title: War and Peace Published
events.blurb: A 41-year-old Russian aristocrat completed the last serial installment of a vast historical novel following five aristocratic families through Russia's Napoleonic Wars. The finished work ran over 1,200 pages and combined personal drama, military history, and a 200-page essay on the philosophy of history tacked onto the end. The author rewrote the opening sentence at least seven times.
events.revealBlurb: 1869 — Leo Tolstoy. It was serialized in the journal Russky Vestnik between 1865 and 1869. Tolstoy later disowned most of his fiction on religious grounds and decades later attempted to destroy his own estate's copyright to prevent his heirs from profiting.

events.title: Treasure Island Published
events.blurb: A 33-year-old Scottish writer, suffering severe pulmonary illness and convalescing in the Scottish Highlands, sketched a treasure map with his 12-year-old stepson on a rainy afternoon and began improvising a story for the boy. The serialized pirate adventure novel that grew from the map — featuring a peg-legged cook, a squawking parrot, a buried fortune, and a black spot — essentially defined the iconography of piracy for the next century and a half.
events.revealBlurb: November 14, 1883 — Robert Louis Stevenson. Initially serialized in the magazine Young Folks in 1881 as "The Sea Cook." The phrase "Shiver me timbers!" does not appear in the book but was popularized by its Long John Silver.

events.title: The Great Gatsby Published
events.blurb: A 28-year-old American novelist published his third novel — a 218-page story about a wealthy bootlegger's obsessive love for an old flame now married to a brutish Yale football star, narrated by a Midwestern newcomer to Long Island. Reviews were respectable; sales were tepid. The author died 15 years later considering himself a failure. The book was rediscovered during WWII when Armed Services Editions shipped 155,000 copies to U.S. soldiers; it is now read in every American high school.
events.revealBlurb: April 10, 1925 — F. Scott Fitzgerald. Original print run: 20,870 copies. Fitzgerald earned $200 in royalties from his fourth novel "Tender Is the Night." His high-schooler daughter Scottie, who detested "The Great Gatsby," left her father's papers to Princeton.

events.title: 1984 Published
events.blurb: A 46-year-old English novelist, suffering from advanced tuberculosis on a remote Scottish island, published a dystopian novel depicting a totalitarian state where history is continuously rewritten, all speech is monitored, and a figurehead leader is omnipresent. He had been working on it for four years; he typed much of it lying in bed. He died of the disease seven months later. The book gave English a vocabulary for surveillance authoritarianism that has never been matched.
events.revealBlurb: June 8, 1949 — George Orwell (Eric Blair). Written on the island of Jura. "Big Brother," "doublethink," "thought police," "Newspeak," and "Orwellian" all entered English usage. The title's year was chosen by reversing 1948, the year he completed the draft.

events.title: Battle of Bunker Hill
events.blurb: American militia who had occupied two hills on a peninsula north of Boston overnight were assaulted by British regulars advancing uphill in three waves. The defenders — reportedly told "don't fire until you see the whites of their eyes" to conserve ammunition — inflicted heavy casualties on the first two waves before running out of powder and being driven from the ground. The British held the field but lost over 1,000 men; the American cause gained enormous moral prestige.
events.revealBlurb: June 17, 1775 — fought mostly on Breed's Hill; misnamed after the adjacent Bunker Hill. British commander: General Thomas Gage. American commander killed in the retreat: General Joseph Warren. Within days, Congress appointed George Washington commander-in-chief.

events.title: Cornwallis Surrenders at Yorktown
events.blurb: A British army of 8,000 men under a peer of the realm, trapped on a Virginia peninsula by a combined Franco-American land force and blocked from the Chesapeake by a French fleet, surrendered after a three-week siege. The British commander, reportedly feigning illness, sent a deputy to the surrender ceremony; his band played a tune called "The World Turned Upside Down." The war dragged on in minor engagements for two more years but the outcome was no longer in doubt.
events.revealBlurb: October 19, 1781 — Lord Cornwallis surrenders to General George Washington and Comte de Rochambeau at Yorktown, Virginia. The French navy's blockade, commanded by Admiral de Grasse, decided the siege. Formal peace negotiations began within months.

events.title: U.S. Constitution Signed
events.blurb: Fifty-five delegates meeting for four months in a Philadelphia state house, working in secret through a sweltering summer with the windows closed against spies, produced a seven-article document replacing the loose Articles of Confederation with a stronger federal framework. Thirty-nine of them signed. An 81-year-old Benjamin Franklin, who had been at nearly every session, pointed at the sun carved into George Washington's chair and said he was finally sure it was rising, not setting.
events.revealBlurb: September 17, 1787 — Independence Hall, Philadelphia. Ratified June 21, 1788 after New Hampshire became the ninth state to approve. The Constitution has been amended 27 times in 235 years — less than once per decade. A different Philadelphia-era document, the Bill of Rights, followed in 1791.

events.title: Coup of 18 Brumaire
events.blurb: A 30-year-old French artillery general, recently returned from an unsuccessful campaign in Egypt, led a coup against the five-man executive Directory that had ruled France for four years. He had political allies in the councils and military support on the ground; within two days the Directory was gone and a new three-consul system was in place with him as its dominant first consul. In name, the revolution continued. In effect, one-man rule had returned.
events.revealBlurb: November 9-10, 1799 — Napoleon Bonaparte at the Château de Saint-Cloud. He would crown himself emperor five years later. The Gregorian-calendar date in the French revolutionary calendar was 18-19 Brumaire, Year VIII.

events.title: Louisiana Purchase Treaty Signed
events.blurb: American negotiators in Paris signed a treaty acquiring roughly 828,000 square miles of territory from France — doubling the size of the United States — for approximately $15 million, or about three cents per acre. The purchase, which Napoleon offered because he needed cash for his European wars, encompassed all or part of fifteen future states and opened the continent to westward expansion.
events.revealBlurb: April 30, 1803 — Paris. Jefferson had only authorized $10 million and was seeking to buy New Orleans alone; Napoleon offered the entire territory. Jefferson privately wondered whether he had constitutional authority to make the deal at all, but bought it anyway. The full price, with interest, came to about $23 million.

events.title: Asteroids Released by Atari
events.blurb: Drawing lines on a vector monitor to simulate drifting through space debris sounds modest. The game that resulted became Atari's best-selling arcade cabinet of all time, pulling in an estimated 10 million quarters per day at its peak. Demand was so extreme that Atari temporarily halted production of other games and shipped Asteroids units inside Lunar Lander cabinets just to get them out the door faster.
events.revealBlurb: November 1979 — Atari released Asteroids in North American arcades. It sold over 70,000 cabinets. The game's high score table was the first widely adopted public performance metric in gaming — and the first subject of documented high-score fraud.

events.title: Nintendo Game Boy Launches in North America
events.blurb: Competing handhelds boasted colour screens and better hardware. Nintendo shipped a grey brick with a pea-green LCD and bundled it with a Soviet puzzle game about falling tetrominoes. The grey brick won. Within weeks every unit in the United States had sold out.
events.revealBlurb: July 31, 1989 — The Game Boy launched in North America at $89.99, selling 40,000 units on day one. The Game Boy line eventually sold 118 million units. The Japan launch had been April 21, 1989.

events.title: The Sims Released
events.blurb: A game in which you build a house and manage the life of a simulated person — feeding them, making them use the bathroom, watching them catch fire if left unattended too long — became the best-selling PC game of the year, and then 2001, and then the best-selling PC game of all time. More than half its players were women, permanently disproving every assumption the games industry held about its audience.
events.revealBlurb: February 4, 2000 — Maxis and EA released The Sims for Windows. It sold 1.77 million copies in North America in its first year. The Sims overtook Myst to become the best-selling PC game ever in 2002. The franchise has sold over 70 million copies.

events.title: Halo: Combat Evolved Launches with Xbox
events.blurb: Microsoft needed a reason for anyone to buy its new video game console from a software company. A science-fiction shooter about a soldier in powered armour became that reason. It sold one million copies faster than any console game in history, perfected twin-stick controller shooting, and made Xbox Live into the template for every online console service that followed.
events.revealBlurb: November 15, 2001 — Halo: Combat Evolved launched as a launch title for the original Xbox. Bungie had originally developed it as a Mac/PC real-time strategy game before Microsoft acquired the studio.

events.title: Minecraft Officially Released
events.blurb: A game with no story, no tutorial, no win state, and graphics that looked like 1989 asked players to punch trees and build whatever they wanted. It became the best-selling video game of all time. Schools adopted it as an educational tool. A generation learned their first lessons about architecture, resource management, and server administration inside it.
events.revealBlurb: November 18, 2011 — Minecraft version 1.0.0 launched at Minecon in Las Vegas. Microsoft acquired developer Mojang in 2014 for $2.5 billion. By 2025 the game had sold over 350 million copies — more than twice the second-best-selling game.

events.title: Transatlantic Telegraph Cable Completed
events.blurb: The steamship Great Eastern finished laying 4,000 kilometres of insulated copper wire across the floor of the Atlantic, connecting Valencia Island, Ireland, to Heart's Content, Newfoundland. The first commercial message crossed in minutes — a journey that had previously taken ten days by ship.

events.title: Suez Canal Opens
events.blurb: The French-designed 193-kilometre sea-level canal linking the Mediterranean to the Red Sea — dug largely by corvée (unpaid forced) Egyptian labour over ten years with massive loss of life — opened to international traffic. A procession of 68 ships led by a French imperial yacht sailed from Port Said to the Red Sea over four days. The canal cut the sea route from London to Bombay by about 7,200 kilometres and shifted the geography of global trade.
events.revealBlurb: November 17, 1869 — designer Ferdinand de Lesseps. Giuseppe Verdi's opera Aida, commissioned by Khedive Ismail for the opening, arrived too late and premiered in 1871. The canal was nationalized by Egypt in 1956, triggering the Suez Crisis.

events.title: Bell Patents Telephone
events.blurb: A 29-year-old Scottish-born American inventor was granted a patent on "the method of, and apparatus for, transmitting vocal or other sounds telegraphically." Three days later he made the first recognized telephone call in his Boston laboratory, summoning his assistant from the next room. The patent, filed the same morning as a rival inventor's competing application, would become the most valuable patent ever issued by the US government.
events.revealBlurb: March 7, 1876 — Alexander Graham Bell. The first call: "Mr. Watson — come here — I want to see you." The rival, Elisha Gray, filed his caveat a few hours later; legal battles continued for years. American Telephone & Telegraph, founded on Bell's patent, became the largest corporation in the world.

events.title: Edison Invents Phonograph
events.blurb: A 30-year-old American inventor shouted the first verse of "Mary Had a Little Lamb" into the horn of a machine he had built at his New Jersey laboratory, then cranked a handle to make the machine play his words back to him. Recording sound — not just transmitting it instantaneously as the telephone did — had never been done before. The device, a tinfoil-cylinder phonograph, would be followed by commercial wax-cylinder versions by the end of the decade.
events.revealBlurb: November 21, 1877 — Thomas Edison at Menlo Park. The original tinfoil phonograph could replay a recording only a few times before the foil wore out. The machine astonished audiences when Edison demonstrated it at the Scientific American office a week later.

events.title: Wright Brothers' First Flight
events.blurb: Two American bicycle-shop owners from Dayton, Ohio achieved the first sustained, controlled, powered flight of a heavier-than-air aircraft on a windswept dune at the Outer Banks of North Carolina. The first flight lasted 12 seconds and covered 36 metres — about the wingspan of a modern commercial airliner. They made three more flights that morning; the fourth covered 260 metres in 59 seconds. Few newspapers reported the achievement; commercial aviation took another three decades to arrive.
events.revealBlurb: December 17, 1903 — Orville and Wilbur Wright at Kill Devil Hills, near Kitty Hawk, NC. The flyer is now in the Smithsonian's National Air and Space Museum. The pair spent 4 years after their first flight battling patent disputes and litigation rather than manufacturing planes.

events.title: Citizen Kane Released
events.blurb: A 25-year-old radio and theatre prodigy made his feature film directing debut with a quasi-biographical study of a newspaper tycoon, structurally organized as a series of flashback interviews about the man's last word ("Rosebud"). The film used deep-focus cinematography, low-angle setups, overlapping dialogue, and non-linear structure in ways that rewrote the cinematic grammar of the next 70 years. Its real-life subject, a media baron, tried to have every print destroyed.
events.revealBlurb: May 1, 1941 — Orson Welles, age 25. The target was William Randolph Hearst, who banned mention of the film in his newspapers. It lost Best Picture to "How Green Was My Valley." It tops nearly every "greatest films of all time" list.

events.title: Bicycle Thieves Released
events.blurb: An Italian director released a quiet 89-minute film about an unemployed working-class man whose stolen bicycle means he cannot take a new job pasting posters on walls. The non-professional actors, documentary-style camera, and refusal of melodramatic conventions defined the Italian neorealist movement. The film spoke for a generation of post-war European audiences who had had enough of Hollywood glamour.
events.revealBlurb: November 24, 1948 — Vittorio De Sica. The father was played by a real factory worker; the son by a young boy De Sica spotted on the street. It won an honorary Academy Award before the foreign language category existed. Its influence on later directors — from Ken Loach to Satyajit Ray — is enormous.

events.title: Seven Samurai Released
events.blurb: A Japanese director released a 207-minute epic about a defenseless farming village that hires seven masterless samurai to protect it from annual bandit raids. The film's action-adventure template — a diverse team of skilled specialists assembled for a dangerous mission — has been imitated in countless subsequent movies across every genre. One of its rainy climactic battles required 18 weeks of shooting and 500 tons of supplemental water.
events.revealBlurb: April 26, 1954 — Akira Kurosawa, starring Toshiro Mifune. The film was remade by Hollywood six years later as "The Magnificent Seven." The 2016 Marvel film "The Avengers" has been called, by its own director, a direct descendant.

events.title: Breathless Released
events.blurb: A 29-year-old French film critic turned director released a 90-minute crime film about a petty thief on the run in Paris with his American girlfriend, shot on handheld camera using natural light, jump cuts, and improvised dialogue. The film's insouciant rulebreaking embodied a new generation of European filmmaking, christened the "Nouvelle Vague" by a critic five years earlier. It made its star into the archetype of post-war cool.
events.revealBlurb: March 16, 1960 — Jean-Luc Godard, starring Jean-Paul Belmondo and Jean Seberg. The famously jarring jump-cuts emerged from an editing crisis: the film was too long and Godard simply removed shots rather than shorten scenes.

events.title: Toy Story Released
events.blurb: A California animation studio released the first feature film produced entirely with computer-generated imagery, a 81-minute buddy comedy about a child's cowboy doll who feels threatened by a new space-ranger action figure. The studio had spent four years on the film, through three near-cancellations and total rewrites; the resulting picture grossed $390 million and established a new production studio as the dominant force in animation for the next two decades.
events.revealBlurb: November 22, 1995 — Pixar Animation Studios, directed by John Lasseter. Tom Hanks and Tim Allen voiced Woody and Buzz Lightyear. Pixar had been Apple founder Steve Jobs's expensive side-project; Disney bought them for $7.4 billion in 2006.

events.title: Pac-Man Debuts in Japanese Arcades
events.blurb: A yellow circle eating dots and fleeing ghosts through a maze seemed like a peculiar bet in an era dominated by shoot-'em-ups. It became the highest-grossing arcade game ever made, the first video game character to achieve mass-market celebrity, and the template for an entirely new genre. Its creator wanted a game that women would actually want to play.
events.revealBlurb: May 22, 1980 — Namco's Puck-Man (renamed Pac-Man for Western markets to prevent vandalism) went on location test in Shibuya, Tokyo. By 1982 an estimated 30 billion quarters had been inserted into Pac-Man machines worldwide.

events.title: Final Fantasy VII Released in Japan
events.blurb: A Japanese role-playing game with pre-rendered 3D backgrounds, full orchestral-style music, and a story involving ecological collapse and corporate villainy sold out PlayStation consoles across Japan before it even launched. On release day it sold 1.75 million copies in a single country in a single day.
events.revealBlurb: January 31, 1997 — Final Fantasy VII launched in Japan for PlayStation. It sold 2.3 million copies in its first three days and over 6 million by 1998. Its western release September 7, 1997, introduced the JRPG genre to millions. The 2020 remake sold over 7 million copies in under four days.

events.title: Half-Life Released by Valve
events.blurb: Every first-person shooter before Half-Life presented missions as separate levels with loading screens and no coherent world. Half-Life placed the player inside a continuous unbroken environment, told its story entirely through actions the player participated in, and won more than 50 Game of the Year awards. Critics later divided gaming history into "pre-Half-Life" and "post-Half-Life" eras.
events.revealBlurb: November 19, 1998 — Valve's debut game released for Windows. Budgeted for lifetime sales of 180,000 copies, it sold 212,000 in the United States alone by year-end and ultimately over 9 million copies. It spawned Counter-Strike as a fan mod. Valve used the revenue to build Steam.

events.title: World of Warcraft Launches
events.blurb: An online game that charged a monthly subscription fee on top of a $50 box price acquired half a million players in its first week and 12 million at its peak — more than the population of several European nations. It swallowed years of people's lives, birthed the term "raiding," generated academic papers about its simulated epidemics, and made "massively multiplayer" a standard genre.
events.revealBlurb: November 23, 2004 — World of Warcraft launched in North America, Australia, and New Zealand. In 2020, researchers cited WoW's 2005 "Corrupted Blood" plague — an accidental in-game epidemic — as a realistic model for studying pandemic behaviour. Lifetime revenue exceeded $9 billion.

events.title: Oculus Rift Kickstarter Campaign Launches
events.blurb: A 19-year-old in his parents' garage had spent years building virtual reality headsets from scavenged parts. His Kickstarter campaign asked for $250,000 to build a developer kit. It raised $2.4 million from nearly 10,000 backers. Two years later, Facebook acquired his company for $2 billion.
events.revealBlurb: August 1, 2012 — Palmer Luckey launched the Oculus Rift Kickstarter, raising 974% of its $250,000 goal. Facebook (now Meta) acquired Oculus VR in March 2014 for approximately $2 billion.

events.title: Caning of Senator Charles Sumner
events.blurb: Representative Preston Brooks of South Carolina strode onto the Senate floor and beat Senator Charles Sumner of Massachusetts unconscious with a metal-topped gutta-percha cane, inflicting such severe head injuries that Sumner could not return to his seat for over three years. The assault came two days after Sumner delivered a blistering antislavery speech mocking Brooks's cousin; Massachusetts left Sumner's empty desk on display as a rebuke.
events.revealBlurb: May 22, 1856 — U.S. Senate chamber. Brooks resigned, was immediately re-elected by South Carolina, and received commemorative canes inscribed "Hit Him Again." Sumner's empty desk served as visible propaganda for the antislavery cause for three years. The incident convinced many Northerners that slavery corrupted men beyond reason.

events.title: Dred Scott Decision
events.blurb: The Supreme Court ruled 7–2 that Dred Scott, an enslaved man who had lived in free states and territories, had no right to sue for his freedom — and that Congress had never possessed the authority to ban slavery from the territories, thereby invalidating the Missouri Compromise. Chief Justice Roger Taney further held that Black Americans, free or enslaved, were not citizens and had "no rights which the white man was bound to respect."
events.revealBlurb: March 6, 1857 — Washington, D.C. The ruling was intended to settle the slavery question definitively; instead it inflamed the North and energized the new Republican Party. Dred Scott was freed by his original owner's family two months after the decision. He died 16 months later, a free man.

events.title: Gettysburg Address Delivered
events.blurb: At the dedication of a military cemetery on the grounds of the bloodiest battle of the war, Abraham Lincoln delivered a 272-word speech that redefined the purpose of the conflict — not merely preserving the Union, but completing the "unfinished work" of the Declaration of Independence by ensuring that a government of the people would not perish. Lincoln spoke for less than two minutes; the main orator that day delivered a two-hour speech that nobody remembers.
events.revealBlurb: November 19, 1863 — Gettysburg, Pennsylvania. The battle four months earlier killed or wounded more than 50,000 men over three days. Edward Everett — the two-hour orator — wrote Lincoln privately: "I should be glad if I could flatter myself that I came as near to the central idea of the occasion, in two hours, as you did in two minutes."

events.title: President Kennedy Assassinated in Dallas
events.blurb: At approximately 12:30 pm that day, President John F. Kennedy was shot in the head while riding in an open motorcade through Dealey Plaza in Dallas, Texas, and was pronounced dead at Parkland Memorial Hospital at 1:00 pm. Lee Harvey Oswald was arrested that afternoon; two days later, Oswald was shot and killed on live national television by nightclub owner Jack Ruby before he could stand trial.
events.revealBlurb: November 22, 1963 — Dallas, Texas. Lyndon Johnson was sworn in as president on Air Force One, with a blood-spattered Jacqueline Kennedy standing beside him. The Warren Commission concluded Oswald acted alone; roughly 60% of Americans have never believed it.

events.title: Watergate Break-In
events.blurb: At 2:30 in the morning, Washington D.C. police arrested five men inside the headquarters of the Democratic National Committee at the Watergate complex, where they had broken in to photograph documents and plant surveillance devices. The burglars were connected to the Committee to Re-Elect the President, and the discovery of the break-in and the subsequent cover-up by the Nixon White House eventually destroyed his presidency.
events.revealBlurb: June 17, 1972 — Watergate complex, Washington, D.C. The burglars were caught because a security guard noticed tape on a door latch and called the police. Nixon won re-election in November 1972 in one of the largest landslides in American history — 520 to 17 electoral votes — while the cover-up was already underway.

events.title: "Who Shot J.R.?" Revealed
events.blurb: An estimated 83 million American viewers — 76 percent of all active television sets at the time — tuned in to a prime-time U.S. soap opera to learn who had fired the cliffhanger-ending shot that had kept the nation guessing for eight months. At the time it was the most-watched single program in television history. Souvenir T-shirts, novelty songs, and betting pools had all sprouted during the summer hiatus between seasons.
events.revealBlurb: November 21, 1980 — Dallas, episode "Who Done It." The shooter was Kristin Shepard, played by Mary Crosby. J.R. Ewing survived. The "Who Shot J.R.?" plot is considered a pioneer of the season-ending cliffhanger in prime-time television.

events.title: Challenger Disintegration
events.blurb: Space Shuttle Challenger broke apart 73 seconds after launch when a rubber O-ring seal on the right solid rocket booster failed in overnight temperatures that had dropped to -8 °C, allowing combustion gases to breach the joint and sever the external tank. All seven crew members were killed, including Christa McAuliffe, who had been selected from more than 11,000 applicants for NASA's Teacher in Space program.
events.revealBlurb: January 28, 1986 — STS-51-L. Engineers at Morton Thiokol had urged a launch delay the night before, citing O-ring behavior in cold temperatures; NASA managers overruled them. The crew cabin survived the initial breakup intact and fell for nearly three minutes before striking the Atlantic at roughly 320 km/h.

events.title: Milli Vanilli Grammy Stripped
events.blurb: The Recording Academy revoked a Grammy award given to a German-based pop duo nine months earlier after the duo's producer, fired in a dispute, revealed publicly that the duo had not actually sung on their multi-platinum album — other studio vocalists had. The two dreadlocked frontmen had been, in effect, models who lip-synced. The scandal ended their careers; the Recording Academy has not revoked a Grammy for any reason since.
events.revealBlurb: November 19, 1990 — Milli Vanilli (Rob Pilatus and Fab Morvan) stripped of their 1989 Best New Artist Grammy. Rob Pilatus was found dead in 1998 at 32 of an accidental overdose. Fab Morvan has continued to perform. The actual vocalists included Charles Shaw, John Davis, and Brad Howell.

events.title: Kurt Cobain Dies
events.blurb: A 27-year-old grunge-rock frontman was found dead of a self-inflicted shotgun wound in the greenhouse above the garage of his Seattle home. He had struggled with heroin addiction, a collapsed marriage, chronic stomach pain, and the deep anxieties of sudden fame. His suicide note quoted a line from a Neil Young song: "It's better to burn out than to fade away." A public memorial at Seattle Center drew 7,000 mourners.
events.revealBlurb: April 5, 1994 — Kurt Cobain of Nirvana. The body was not discovered for three days, by an electrician installing a security system. Conspiracy theories have persisted for decades. Cobain joined the "27 Club" of pop musicians who died at that age, including Jimi Hendrix, Janis Joplin, Jim Morrison, and Amy Winehouse.

events.title: Seinfeld Finale
events.blurb: The 180th and final episode of a nine-year NBC sitcom about petty New York narcissists aired to 76 million viewers. The divisive finale had the four main characters put on trial in a fictional Massachusetts town for failing to help a carjacking victim, watched by a parade of minor characters from earlier seasons who had been wronged by them. Critics and fans were largely disappointed; its creator defended it as consistent with the show's amoral premise.
events.revealBlurb: May 14, 1998 — "The Finale." Written by Larry David, returning after leaving the show in 1996. Ad slots on the finale sold for around $2 million for 30 seconds — a pre-Super Bowl record for a TV program.

events.title: The Hijra
events.blurb: Fleeing plots against his life in the Arabian trading city where he had preached for 13 years, a 53-year-old prophet and roughly seventy of his followers slipped out at night and rode 320 kilometres north to a rival oasis town whose feuding tribes had invited him to mediate. He arrived to a welcoming reception and began building the first Islamic community under his political authority.
events.revealBlurb: July 16, 622 — Muhammad's migration from Mecca to Medina. The Islamic calendar begins from this year, not his birth. "Hijra" literally means "emigration" or "severing of ties."

events.title: Battle of Tours
events.blurb: A Frankish mayor of the palace led an infantry army into a defensive wall of shields against a much larger Umayyad cavalry force that had been raiding deep into western Europe. The battle's outcome stopped the northward expansion of the Islamic caliphate into the Frankish heartland and established the Carolingian dynasty as the dominant power of the region.
events.revealBlurb: October 10, 732 — Charles Martel ("Charles the Hammer") in central France. His grandson Charlemagne would be crowned emperor 68 years later. Edward Gibbon later wrote that without the victory, "the interpretation of the Koran would now be taught in the schools of Oxford."

events.title: Battle of Hastings
events.blurb: A Norman duke from across the English Channel invaded a southern English kingdom with 7,000 men, met its exhausted king — who had marched south after defeating a Norwegian invasion three weeks earlier in the north — on a hillside near the coast, and won in an all-day battle. The English king was killed, reportedly by an arrow through the eye. The victor replaced the Anglo-Saxon aristocracy with his own.
events.revealBlurb: October 14, 1066 — William the Conqueror vs. Harold Godwinson near the town of Battle, East Sussex. The Bayeux Tapestry, a 70-metre embroidered account, was sewn within a decade. Modern English is still 50–60 percent French-derived because of the resulting Norman elite.

events.title: Council of Clermont
events.blurb: The pope, addressing a crowd of French clergy and nobles in an open field outside a central French city after a church council, called on Christendom to take up arms and march east to recover a holy land from Muslim rule. "Deus vult," the crowd cried back — "God wills it." Within three years, 100,000 pilgrims and knights would be on the road.
events.revealBlurb: November 27, 1095 — Pope Urban II. His stated goals shifted in each retelling; the Byzantine emperor had only asked for mercenaries. The First Crusade's armies would surprise everyone, including themselves, by actually reaching Jerusalem.

events.title: Battle of Crécy
events.blurb: An outnumbered English army of longbowmen and dismounted knights, arrayed behind earthworks on a hillside in northern France, destroyed a confident French chivalric force that charged uphill through their own crossbowmen. The battle demonstrated that skilled commoner archers could annihilate mounted aristocracy, and it made the English longbow the most feared weapon in Europe for the next seventy years.
events.revealBlurb: August 26, 1346 — Edward III and the Black Prince, early Hundred Years' War. The blind king of Bohemia, fighting on the French side, asked his knights to tie his horse to theirs so he could strike one blow. They did; he did; they all died together.

events.title: First Public Film Screening
events.blurb: Two French brothers, sons of a portrait photographer, held the first commercial screening of projected motion pictures in the basement of a Paris café. The audience of 33 paid one franc each to watch ten short films — workers leaving a factory, a baby being fed, a boat leaving a harbor. Their cinematograph was both camera and projector; the film was 35mm. Within a year their operators were touring every continent.
events.revealBlurb: December 28, 1895 — Louis and Auguste Lumière at the Salon Indien du Grand Café, Paris. The apocryphal story that audiences ran screaming from the train-arriving film comes from a later screening. The Lumières thought cinema was "an invention without a future" and quickly moved on to other projects.

events.title: Metropolis Released
events.blurb: A 36-year-old Austrian director released a 153-minute silent epic — at the time the most expensive film ever made — set in a stratified future city where wealthy elites enjoy skyscraper gardens above an underground inferno of machine-tending workers. The film's visual language — robot maidens, neon skylines, expressionist sets — shaped science-fiction imagery for the next century. The premiere had uneven reception; 40 minutes of footage were later cut.
events.revealBlurb: January 10, 1927 — Fritz Lang at the UFA-Palast am Zoo, Berlin. A reasonably complete version was pieced together only in 2008, when a 16mm print from the 1930s was found in a Buenos Aires archive. The robot Maria was voted the most important film robot in history.

events.title: Casablanca Premieres
events.blurb: A wartime romance set in a Moroccan cafe — produced on a tight schedule with an often-improvised script — premiered at a New York theater two weeks after Allied troops actually landed in the real-life city, a coincidence that boosted interest. The film's lead actor and actress had expected it to be a forgettable assignment; its dialogue's half-dozen phrases would be quoted by a century of audiences. Neither of the two stars was anyone's first choice for their parts.
