events.revealBlurb: November 26, 1942 — Hollywood Theatre, NYC. Director Michael Curtiz, stars Humphrey Bogart and Ingrid Bergman. "Here's looking at you, kid" was Bogart's improvisation. "Play it again, Sam" is never actually said in the film.

events.title: Rashomon Released
events.blurb: A 40-year-old Japanese director released a 88-minute film in which the same violent encounter is recounted by four different participants, none of whom agrees with any of the others. The Venice Film Festival awarded it the Golden Lion the following year, and the world film industry discovered Japanese cinema as a major force. The very title became an English noun: "the Rashomon effect" is the concept of contradictory memories.
events.revealBlurb: August 26, 1950 — Akira Kurosawa. The producers were reportedly baffled by the script and wanted it re-edited. Its Venice win completely blindsided Japanese critics, who had not thought much of the film. It led directly to the global reception of Ozu, Mizoguchi, and Kurosawa's later work.

events.title: The Godfather Released
events.blurb: A 32-year-old American director of partial Italian descent, working on his third feature, released a 175-minute adaptation of a recent mass-market novel about an Italian-American crime family. His studio had imposed cast, budget, and length conditions throughout production; it had also tried to fire him multiple times. The film grossed more than any previous picture in history, won Best Picture, and launched decades of imitators that have never quite matched it.
events.revealBlurb: March 14, 1972 — Francis Ford Coppola. Marlon Brando's sagging jowls were created with dental plumpers; Al Pacino's casting was fought bitterly by Paramount executives who wanted Ryan O'Neal. The horse's head was real — acquired from a dog-food plant.

events.title: Netscape IPO
events.blurb: A 16-month-old Silicon Valley company that had distributed free web browsers and had never turned a profit went public at $28 a share, opened at $71, and closed its first trading day at $58.25. Its 24-year-old co-founder was suddenly worth $58 million on paper. Wall Street had discovered the internet, and the next five years of stock-market mania had a starting gun.
events.revealBlurb: August 9, 1995 — Netscape Communications. Co-founder Marc Andreessen ended up on the cover of Time two years later with the caption "The Kid Who Tamed the Web." Microsoft's bundled Internet Explorer would eventually kill Netscape; the company sold to AOL in 1999.

events.title: iTunes Store Launched
events.blurb: A California computer company launched an online music store selling individual songs for 99 cents each, a pricing decision its CEO had to personally negotiate with record-label executives deeply suspicious of any further internet disruption. The store sold a million downloads in its first six days. Within four years, it was the largest music retailer in the United States.
events.revealBlurb: April 28, 2003 — Apple. Steve Jobs had threaten to "pull the plug" on the negotiations at one point. The catalogue launched with 200,000 songs, Mac-only; Windows compatibility came in October. The per-song price model reshaped the music industry.

events.title: Instagram Launched
events.blurb: A two-person startup released a free iOS app that let users take photos, apply one of eleven retro filters, and share them to a simple timeline-based social network. It acquired 25,000 users on launch day and its first million within three months. Facebook bought the company for $1 billion in cash and stock eighteen months later, when it had thirteen employees and zero revenue.
events.revealBlurb: October 6, 2010 — Kevin Systrom and Mike Krieger. Originally built as a location-based check-in app called Burbn. The $1 billion Facebook acquisition in April 2012 is now considered one of the great bargains in tech history.

events.title: WikiLeaks Cablegate
events.blurb: A whistleblower-platform website and a consortium of five newspapers began publishing, in coordinated waves, 251,287 U.S. diplomatic cables leaked by a 22-year-old U.S. Army intelligence analyst. The cables ranged from the mundane to the explosive — unflattering private assessments of world leaders, evidence of corruption in allied governments, and revelations about civilian deaths in Iraq and Afghanistan. The leaker would face the longest sentence ever imposed for leaking U.S. government information.
events.revealBlurb: November 28, 2010 — leaker Chelsea Manning (then Bradley), sentenced to 35 years in 2013. Obama commuted her sentence in 2017. WikiLeaks founder Julian Assange lived in the Ecuadorian embassy in London from 2012 until 2019; he was released from UK custody in a 2024 plea deal.

events.title: ChatGPT Launched
events.blurb: A San Francisco AI research lab released, as an unassuming "research preview," a conversational interface to its large language model. The chatbot could answer questions, write essays, debug code, and generate poetry in response to natural-language prompts. It gained a hundred million monthly users within two months — making it the fastest-growing consumer product in history. Incumbent tech giants pivoted their entire product strategies within weeks.
events.revealBlurb: November 30, 2022 — OpenAI. The underlying model, GPT-3.5, had existed for months; the chat wrapper made all the difference. By 2025, generative AI had become a ~$200 billion global industry. Anthropic, Google, Meta, and xAI joined OpenAI as frontier labs.

events.title: Ptolemy's Almagest Completed
events.blurb: A Greco-Roman astronomer working in Alexandria compiled the most comprehensive mathematical model of the heavens yet assembled, describing the apparent motions of the Sun, Moon, planets, and 1,022 fixed stars using a system of circles and epicycles centred on the Earth. The work synthesised centuries of Babylonian and Greek observations and provided a predictive model accurate enough to calculate planetary positions centuries into the future.
events.revealBlurb: c. 150 CE — the Almagest was so complete that it suppressed further progress in astronomy for over a millennium. Astronomers kept patching it rather than questioning its Earth-centred premise. The name comes from the Arabic al-majisṭī, meaning "the greatest" — added by Islamic scholars who translated and preserved the text when European copies were lost.

events.title: Galileo Maps the Moon
events.blurb: An Italian natural philosopher directed a 20× magnification tube skyward and produced detailed drawings of the Moon's surface, revealing mountains and craters rather than a perfect celestial sphere as ancient philosophy held. He calculated the heights of lunar mountains by measuring the lengths of the shadows they cast.

events.title: On the Origin of Species Published
events.blurb: A 502-page book argued that all species of life descended from common ancestors through a process of natural selection, where individuals with heritable traits better suited to their environment survived and reproduced at higher rates. The first print run of 1,250 copies sold out to booksellers on the day it was offered for sale.
events.revealBlurb: November 24, 1859 — Darwin had sat on the theory for twenty years, terrified of the controversy. He finally rushed it to press only after Alfred Russel Wallace independently wrote him a letter describing the same mechanism. The two men's papers were presented jointly to the Linnean Society in 1858.

events.title: Pulsars Discovered
events.blurb: A graduate student mapping the sky with a radio telescope noticed a repeating pulse of radio waves arriving with uncanny regularity every 1.33 seconds — far too precise to be natural noise. The signal was briefly nicknamed "LGM-1" (Little Green Men) until other examples were found across the sky, establishing a new class of rapidly rotating neutron stars more accurate than any clock then built.
events.revealBlurb: November 28, 1967 — Jocelyn Bell Burnell spotted the anomaly in paper chart rolls she had to check by hand. Her supervisor Antony Hewish and astronomer Martin Ryle shared the 1974 Nobel Prize in Physics for the discovery; Bell Burnell was excluded despite being the one who found it, in what became one of science's most-debated Nobel omissions.

events.title: Dolly the Sheep — First Cloned Mammal Announced
events.blurb: Scientists at a Scottish research institute announced the birth of a sheep cloned from a cell taken from an adult mammal's mammary gland — the first time a complex animal had been produced from a fully differentiated adult cell rather than an embryo. The achievement overturned a long-held belief that the DNA in adult cells had irreversibly lost its potential to generate a whole organism.
events.revealBlurb: February 22, 1997 — Dolly was born months earlier but kept secret while the team gathered data and published. She was named after the country singer Dolly Parton, because the cell donor was a mammary gland cell. Dolly developed arthritis and a lung disease unusually early, raising questions about whether cloned animals age faster — still debated today.

events.title: Munich Agreement
events.blurb: Four heads of government met through the night in a grand hall in southern Europe and handed over a democratic nation's border region to an aggressive neighbour — without inviting a single representative of that nation to the table. The leader who returned home waving the signed paper declared it meant peace; within six months the entire country had been swallowed.
events.revealBlurb: September 30, 1938 — Chamberlain, Daladier, Hitler, and Mussolini signed over the Sudetenland at 1:30 AM. Chamberlain's "peace for our time" paper became history's most mocked diplomatic document. Czechoslovakia's envoys waited in an anteroom and were simply informed of the result.

events.title: Invasion of Poland
events.blurb: At 4:43 in the morning a warship opened fire on a peninsula garrison, and within minutes armoured columns and aircraft were crossing a national border along a 1,600-kilometre front from three directions simultaneously. Two days later, two of the invader's neighbours declared war — and the world's largest conflict had begun.
events.revealBlurb: September 1, 1939 — the battleship Schleswig-Holstein fired the first shots at Westerplatte. The 88-man garrison held out for seven days against a force many times its size. Poland was split between Germany and the Soviet Union by October 6; a government-in-exile continued the fight from London.

events.title: Scuttling of the Graf Spee
events.blurb: A feared commerce-raider that had sunk nine merchant ships in three months limped into a neutral harbour for repairs after a running battle with three smaller cruisers, then sat immobile while international diplomacy set a 72-hour countdown. Twenty thousand spectators lined the waterfront to watch her captain make his final decision.
events.revealBlurb: December 17, 1939, Montevideo. Captain Hans Langsdorff scuttled the Admiral Graf Spee at 8:55 PM rather than risk his crew in what he believed was an overwhelming British trap. Three days later he wrapped himself in the ship's battle ensign and shot himself. The trap was largely bluff.

events.title: First Nuclear Chain Reaction
events.blurb: In a squash court beneath a university stadium, a team of physicists assembled 45,000 carefully machined blocks of graphite around pellets of uranium into a lattice the size of a house, withdrew a control rod, and achieved humanity's first self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction — completing the key step toward a new category of weapon.
events.revealBlurb: December 2, 1942, under Stagg Field at the University of Chicago. Enrico Fermi's team celebrated with a bottle of Chianti in paper cups. The coded telegram sent to Washington read: "The Italian navigator has just landed in the New World." The reactor sat in a populated neighbourhood with no containment vessel.

events.title: Tehran Conference
events.blurb: The three most powerful leaders of the opposing alliance met for the first time in a capital city in southwest Asia, committing to a firm timeline for a massive cross-channel invasion in spring, agreeing on the postwar borders of one eastern European nation, and beginning to sketch the political shape of the world that would follow the conflict.
events.revealBlurb: November 28 – December 1, 1943 — FDR, Churchill, and Stalin met in Tehran. It was the first time FDR and Stalin met in person. Roosevelt, whose security staff feared assassination, moved into the Soviet Embassy at Stalin's suggestion — and Soviet intelligence promptly bugged his suite. Churchill celebrated his 69th birthday at the conference with a dinner attended by all three leaders.

events.title: Indian Independence & Partition
events.blurb: At the stroke of midnight, two new independent dominions came into existence on the subcontinent — one majority-Hindu, one majority-Muslim — as the British flag was lowered on the largest and oldest of Britain's imperial possessions. The division of provinces along religious lines displaced between 10 and 20 million people, and perhaps a million died in the communal violence that followed.
events.revealBlurb: August 14-15, 1947 — Pakistan on the 14th, India on the 15th. The boundary lines had been drawn by a London barrister, Cyril Radcliffe, who had never visited the subcontinent and had 36 days to complete the task. Nehru's "Tryst with Destiny" speech was delivered at midnight from the Constituent Assembly.

events.title: Rajiv Gandhi Assassinated
events.blurb: A former prime minister, campaigning for his return to office at a rally in a south Indian town, bent to accept a garland from a young woman in the crowd. A belt of explosives strapped to her waist detonated, killing him, her, and sixteen others. He was 46. She was a Tamil Tiger suicide bomber avenging his government's military intervention in Sri Lanka four years earlier.
events.revealBlurb: May 21, 1991 — Sriperumbudur, Tamil Nadu. The bomber was Thenmozhi Rajaratnam, code-named "Dhanu." Election campaigning was suspended; his party won a sympathy vote and formed the next government, but without a Gandhi in sight for the first time since independence.

events.title: Economic Liberalization
events.blurb: Facing a balance-of-payments crisis so acute that the country had airlifted 47 tonnes of its gold reserves to London as collateral, a new finance minister presented a budget that systematically dismantled the license-permit-quota economy that had governed Indian business for four decades. Industrial licensing was abolished, imports liberalized, foreign investment welcomed. The economy would nearly quintuple over the next two decades.
events.revealBlurb: July 24, 1991 — Finance Minister Manmohan Singh's budget speech. Prime Minister Narasimha Rao provided the political cover. Singh, invoking Victor Hugo, declared: "No power on Earth can stop an idea whose time has come."

events.title: Kargil War
events.blurb: Pakistani soldiers, disguised as local insurgents, occupied high-altitude ridges inside the Indian-administered portion of a disputed northern territory over the winter. Their discovery by a shepherd in early May touched off a 74-day war fought at elevations up to 5,600 metres. India retook the peaks one by one with heavy infantry losses; Pakistan, pressured by Washington, withdrew.
events.revealBlurb: May 3 to July 26, 1999 — the Line of Control in Kargil, Ladakh. The conflict was one of the first televised wars in India. Captain Vikram Batra became a national hero before dying on Point 4875 on July 7.

events.title: 26/11 Mumbai Attacks
events.blurb: Ten men trained by a Pakistan-based militant group landed at a fishing harbour in the country's financial capital by rubber dinghy after hijacking an Indian fishing trawler at sea, and fanned out across the city to attack a railway station, a Jewish centre, a café, and two luxury hotels. The resulting sieges lasted 60 hours. 166 people died and more than 300 were wounded. Nine attackers were killed; the sole survivor was captured, tried, and hanged four years later.
events.revealBlurb: November 26-29, 2008 — Mumbai. The captured gunman, Ajmal Kasab, was hanged on November 21, 2012. The attacks were coordinated over satellite phone from Karachi; the operational planner, Sajid Mir, was finally convicted in Pakistan in 2022.

events.title: 15th Amendment Ratified
events.blurb: A constitutional amendment prohibiting the denial of voting rights "on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude" was ratified, giving Black men the theoretical right to vote. Within three decades, poll taxes, literacy tests, grandfather clauses, and organized terror had effectively erased Black voting across the former Confederacy.
events.revealBlurb: February 3, 1870. It took the Voting Rights Act of 1965 — 95 years later — to make the amendment's promise practical. Black women were excluded not by race but by sex until the 19th Amendment in 1920.

events.title: Military Desegregation Order
events.blurb: A U.S. president signed an executive order mandating "equality of treatment and opportunity" in the armed forces without regard to race, color, religion, or national origin. The army resisted for nearly five years; full integration of combat units was not achieved until the Korean War made ignoring Black replacements impossible.
events.revealBlurb: July 26, 1948 — Executive Order 9981, Harry Truman. He signed it partly out of conviction, partly because Black voters in northern cities were now pivotal to Democratic victory. The last all-Black unit was dissolved in 1954.

events.title: Rosa Parks Arrested
events.blurb: A 42-year-old department-store seamstress and longtime NAACP secretary refused to give up her seat on a city bus in an Alabama capital when the white section filled up and the driver demanded the first row of Black seating. She was arrested for violating municipal segregation ordinances. The local Black community organized a one-day bus boycott that became a 381-day boycott.
events.revealBlurb: December 1, 1955 — Montgomery, Alabama. Parks was not, as legend has it, "too tired" to move — she was a trained activist who had attended a civil rights training school months earlier. Her act was calculated. A 26-year-old new preacher in town, Martin Luther King Jr., was chosen to lead the boycott.

events.title: Montgomery Bus Boycott Ends
events.blurb: After 381 days of Black residents walking, carpooling, and riding Black-owned taxis rather than boarding segregated city buses, the U.S. Supreme Court upheld a lower-court ruling that bus segregation was unconstitutional. The next morning, Martin Luther King Jr. and Rosa Parks boarded an integrated bus in the front seats. The boycott had nearly bankrupted the transit system.
events.revealBlurb: December 20, 1956 — Martin Luther King rose to national prominence via the boycott. The organizing bureau ran car-pool lots that transported 30,000 people a day. Many Black women walked miles to work for over a year. "My feet is tired," one said famously, "but my soul is rested."

events.title: Birmingham Children's Crusade
events.blurb: Over several days in a notoriously segregated Alabama steel city, more than a thousand Black schoolchildren — some as young as 6 — marched out of classes in organized protest. Police commissioner Bull Connor ordered fire hoses and attack dogs deployed against them. Photographs of a teenage boy lunged at by a German shepherd appeared on front pages across the world.
events.revealBlurb: May 2-5, 1963 — Birmingham, Alabama. King agreed to use children over the objections of many advisers; they were less vulnerable to losing jobs for protesting. Within weeks, the Kennedy administration introduced what became the Civil Rights Act.

events.title: Vesalius Publishes De Fabrica
events.blurb: A 28-year-old Flemish anatomist at the University of Padua published a lavishly illustrated seven-volume atlas of human anatomy based on dissections he had performed personally, often on the bodies of recently executed criminals. Many of the 273 woodcut illustrations contradicted established Galenic teachings on points ranging from the structure of the jawbone to the absence of a hole between the heart's chambers. The book launched anatomy as a modern evidence-based science.
events.revealBlurb: 1543 — Andreas Vesalius, "De Humani Corporis Fabrica." The illustrations were probably drawn by students of Titian. Vesalius' enemies in traditional medical faculties fought him bitterly; he burned his own unpublished work in despair at one point and entered court life, dying on a pilgrimage 21 years later.

events.title: First Ether Anesthesia Demo
events.blurb: A Boston dentist administered inhaled diethyl ether vapour to a patient in the surgical amphitheatre of Massachusetts General Hospital, rendering him unconscious while a leading surgeon removed a tumour from his neck. The patient woke pain-free. The surgeon turned to the assembled observers and said, "Gentlemen, this is no humbug." Surgical anesthesia had arrived; the previous era of surgery as fast, agonizing amputations in the patient's full consciousness was ending.
events.revealBlurb: October 16, 1846 — dentist William T. G. Morton and surgeon John Collins Warren at MGH, Boston. The amphitheatre, now called the "Ether Dome," is preserved as a National Historic Landmark. Morton spent the rest of his life in failed litigation trying to collect royalties on the technique.

events.title: Pasteur's Rabies Vaccine Used on a Human
events.blurb: A French chemist administered the first human dose of an experimental rabies treatment to a nine-year-old boy who had been severely bitten by a rabid dog two days earlier and faced certain death without intervention. The boy survived, and the successful case launched the practice of post-exposure vaccination for infectious disease.

events.title: First Human Heart Transplant
events.blurb: A South African surgeon transplanted the heart of a 25-year-old accident victim into a 53-year-old grocer in a nine-hour operation at Groote Schuur Hospital in Cape Town. The recipient survived 18 days before dying of pneumonia; the same surgical team performed a second transplant 13 days later — that patient lived 19 months.

events.title: First Heart Transplant
events.blurb: A South African surgeon led a nine-hour operation at a Cape Town hospital transplanting the heart of a 25-year-old woman, killed by a car striking her as she crossed the road to buy cake, into the chest of a 54-year-old man with severe coronary disease. The patient lived 18 days before dying of pneumonia. The surgeon instantly became internationally famous; subsequent transplant patients lived increasingly long with improved immunosuppression.
events.revealBlurb: December 3, 1967 — Christiaan Barnard at Groote Schuur Hospital, Cape Town. Patient: Louis Washkansky. Donor: Denise Darvall. Barnard's second patient, Philip Blaiberg, lived 19 months. The 5-year survival rate for heart transplants is now about 75 percent.

events.title: Pong Released in Arcades
events.blurb: A black-and-white rectangle containing two paddles and a bouncing dot was installed in a Sunnyvale, California tavern as a hardware test. The test machine broke within days — not from malfunction, but because the coin slot had overflowed with quarters. Atari scrambled to ship units nationwide, and the commercial video game industry was born.
events.revealBlurb: November 29, 1972 — Atari Inc., founded that June by Nolan Bushnell and Ted Dabney, shipped Pong to arcades. The Andy Capp's Tavern prototype jammed after a week because it held too many coins.

events.title: Atari 2600 Launches
events.blurb: For the first time, a home console used interchangeable cartridges — meaning the same hardware could play a new game every week. Atari sold 250,000 units in the first months at $199 apiece. Within three years the living room had replaced the arcade as the primary venue for video games.
events.revealBlurb: September 11, 1977 — Atari released the Video Computer System (renamed 2600 in 1982). By 1982, 15 million 2600s had been sold and the console was generating $2 billion in annual revenue.

events.title: North American Video Game Crash
events.blurb: The home video game market had grown so fast that no one noticed it had filled up with garbage. Retailers were buried in unsold cartridges, consumers had lost all trust, and by 1985 an industry that had been worth $3.2 billion two years earlier had collapsed to $100 million — a 97 percent decline. Atari buried millions of unsold cartridges in a New Mexico landfill.
events.revealBlurb: 1983–1985 — Annual revenue fell from $3.2 billion (1983) to approximately $100 million (1985). The Atari landfill in Alamogordo, New Mexico — long an urban legend — was excavated in April 2014 and confirmed to contain millions of E.T. cartridges.

events.title: Super Mario Bros. Released in Japan
events.blurb: A moustachioed Italian plumber leaping over mushrooms and sliding down pipes became the defining character of interactive entertainment. The game shipped as a pack-in with the Nintendo Entertainment System and single-handedly revived an industry that had collapsed two years earlier under the weight of its own shovelware.
events.revealBlurb: September 13, 1985 — Super Mario Bros. launched for Nintendo's Famicom in Japan. It sold over 40 million copies, a record that stood until Wii Sports in 2009. Designer Shigeru Miyamoto built the entire world around the mechanic of a running jump.

events.title: Counter-Strike Released as Standalone
events.blurb: Two amateur developers built a modification for Half-Life in which terrorists and counter-terrorists fought in small tactical maps. Valve noticed the mod's download numbers, purchased the rights, and released it as a standalone product. It became the most-played online game in the world for over a decade, the game credited with institutionalising competitive PC gaming.
events.revealBlurb: November 9, 2000 — Counter-Strike version 1.0 released as a free Half-Life modification. Creators Minh "Gooseman" Le and Jess Cliffe had started the mod in June 1999. In 2023, CS:GO/CS2 peaked at over 1.8 million concurrent Steam players.

events.title: Mozart's Requiem Unfinished
events.blurb: A 35-year-old Austrian composer who had been commissioned by a mysterious stranger six months earlier to compose a requiem Mass for an anonymous client died in his Vienna apartment with the work unfinished. Much of the "Dies irae" and "Lacrimosa" had been sketched only. His widow, in desperate financial circumstances, had a student complete the work to secure the remaining half of the commission fee.
events.revealBlurb: December 5, 1791 — Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, aged 35. The mysterious stranger was Count Walsegg, who meant to pass the work off as his own for his late wife. Mozart's student Franz Xaver Süssmayr completed it; his contributions have been debated ever since.

events.title: The Rite of Spring Riot
events.blurb: A 30-year-old Russian composer's ballet score, depicting a pagan spring ritual with jagged rhythms, dissonant chord stacks, and primitivist choreography, premiered at a new Paris theatre and nearly caused a full-scale audience riot. Shouts, whistles, and fistfights broke out within minutes; the choreographer had to shout counts to dancers from the wings because they couldn't hear the orchestra. The piece is now considered one of the pivotal works of 20th-century music.
events.revealBlurb: May 29, 1913 — Igor Stravinsky and Ballets Russes at Théâtre des Champs-Élysées, Paris. Choreography by Vaslav Nijinsky. The Parisian critic Carl Van Vechten reported his seat-neighbour beating rhythmically on his head with his fists in distress.

events.title: First Jazz Recording
events.blurb: Five white musicians from New Orleans, working under the slightly misspelled name "Original Dixieland Jass Band," recorded two sides for a Victor label at a New York studio: "Livery Stable Blues" and "Dixie Jass Band One Step." The 78 sold a million copies, breaking sales records, and introduced the word "jazz" to most Americans. Black New Orleans musicians had been playing the style for years; the first commercial recording went to imitators.
events.revealBlurb: February 26, 1917 — recorded in NYC; released March 7, 1917. The ODJB's cornetist Nick LaRocca later claimed, implausibly, to have invented jazz. The ethical irony of white performers first commercializing a Black art form was noted at the time and has only grown.

events.title: Rhapsody in Blue Premieres
events.blurb: A 25-year-old former Tin Pan Alley song-plugger's first major concert work — a one-movement concerto for piano and jazz band — premiered at a Manhattan concert hall advertised as "An Experiment in Modern Music." The piece's opening clarinet glissando, improvised in rehearsal as a joke, was left in. The concert had begun with banal novelty pieces; by the time the composer walked out to sit at the piano, the audience was dozing. He woke them up.
events.revealBlurb: February 12, 1924 — George Gershwin at Aeolian Hall, Manhattan. The bandleader was Paul Whiteman. The audience included Rachmaninoff, Stravinsky, Fritz Kreisler, and Sergei Rachmaninoff. United Airlines has used it as its ad music since 1987.

events.title: Thriller Released
events.blurb: A 24-year-old singer released his sixth studio album, a collection of nine tracks deliberately designed so every one could be a single. The 14-minute title track's horror-film music video, featuring choreographed zombie dancing, premiered the following December on a cable channel that had until recently been reluctant to play Black artists. The album became, and remains, the best-selling album of all time.
events.revealBlurb: November 30, 1982 — Michael Jackson, produced by Quincy Jones. It has sold over 70 million copies worldwide. The moonwalk, which Jackson debuted performing "Billie Jean" at Motown's 25th-anniversary TV special 3.5 months after release, was not actually his invention.
